# Brake fluid doesn't move in the master cylinder container

When you bleed a hydraulic clutch system on a vehicle like the Toyota Corolla E120, you are dealing with a shared reservoir design that often confuses mechanics. The symptoms you describedâdark black fluid, followed by a soft pedal and a complete lack of pressure transfer to the slave cylinderâare classic indicators of an internal seal failure or a blockage within the master cylinder itself. However, there is a specific mechanical nuance regarding fluid movement in these reservoirs that needs clarification before attempting another bleed attempt.

The issue you identified, where fluid does not flow into the compartment dedicated to the clutch master cylinder despite the reservoir being common for both brakes and clutch, points to a restriction or a failure of the internal check valve mechanism. In many dual-function master cylinders, there is a specific diaphragm or valve that separates the brake section from the clutch section. When you see fluid sitting in one side but not moving to the other, it usually means the internal passage is obstructed or the seal has degraded.

Attempting to bleed this system again by simply opening the slave cylinder bleeder valve will likely yield no results if the master cylinder cannot push fluid through that internal partition. The soft pedal indicates that the piston in the master cylinder might be collapsing under pressure, or the seals are worn out, preventing the hydraulic force generated by your foot from being transmitted effectively. Even if you manage to purge air from the slave side, the system remains non-functional because the primary actuator (the master cylinder) is compromised.

The most logical diagnosis here is that the master cylinder requires replacement. The fact that fluid was dark black before the bleed suggests contamination or overheating of the hydraulic fluid, which can accelerate the degradation of rubber seals. Once those seals fail, the internal geometry often changes, leading to the "blocked" feeling you observed where fluid refuses to cross over to the clutch compartment.

Trying to disassemble a master cylinder on a shared reservoir unit is generally ill-advised for several reasons. First, the internal check valves are fragile and difficult to reseat correctly without factory tolerances. Second, even if you manage to clear the blockage, the worn seals will not hold pressure in the clutch circuit independently of the brake circuit. The trade-off between attempting a repair versus replacing the unit is heavily weighted toward replacement; the labor cost of removing and reinstalling the assembly often exceeds the price of a new part, and the risk of recurring failure remains high.

Before committing to the replacement, ensure you have flushed the entire system with fresh fluid. The black color indicates significant contamination that could damage a newly installed master cylinder or slave cylinder immediately upon reassembly. Drain all remaining fluid from both the brake and clutch lines, inspect the slave cylinder for external leaks or damaged seals, and refill the reservoir with the correct DOT specification fluid (typically DOT 3 or DOT 4 depending on your specific Corolla model year requirements).

Once the system is flushed, install a new master cylinder. Reassemble the pedal linkage carefully, ensuring the pushrod is correctly seated in the slave cylinder before tightening any bolts, as misalignment can cause binding and premature wear. After installation, perform a thorough bleed of the clutch system again. If the fluid flows freely from the slave cylinder bleeder valve upon pumping the pedal with the bleeder closed, and the pedal feels firm, the hydraulic circuit is restored.

If you find that fluid still does not move between the compartments after replacement, there may be an issue with the reservoir cap or a specific venting problem, though this is less common than internal seal failure. In rare cases where the master cylinder housing itself is cracked or the internal divider valve is physically obstructed by debris (like the black sludge mentioned), cleaning the area around the bleed nipple and ensuring no foreign matter entered the system during the initial bleeding process might be necessary. However, given the age of the vehicle and the condition of the fluid, a full component replacement is the most reliable path forward.
